name: IRA

summary: Supply the current age, the retirement age, the tax bracket at retirement and the annual contribution and the IRA calculator solves for tax bracket during contribution. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the IRA calculator work?
sections.html:
The IRA calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports tax bracket during contribution in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the current age, the retirement age, the tax bracket at retirement and the annual contribution.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the IRA calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Tax bracket during contribution=(annual contribution − annual contribution after tax (Roth IRA)) ÷ annual contribution
Contribution years=-current age + retirement age
Contribution years=the natural log of ((annual contribution × annual return rate + annual contribution + IRA balance × annual return rate) ÷ (annual contribution × (annual return rate + 1))) ÷ the natural log of (annual return rate + 1)
Contribution years=the natural log of ((annual contribution after tax (Roth IRA) × annual return rate + annual contribution after tax (Roth IRA) + annual return rate × roth IRA balance) ÷ (annual contribution after tax (Roth IRA) × (annual return rate + 1))) ÷ the natural log of (annual return rate + 1)
Years of withdrawals=the natural log of (IRA annual withdrawal × (annual return rate + 1) ÷ (IRA annual withdrawal × annual return rate + IRA annual withdrawal − IRA balance × annual return rate)) ÷ the natural log of (annual return rate + 1)
Annual withdrawal after tax=IRA annual withdrawal × tax bracket at retirement

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The IRA calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the current age, the retirement age and the tax bracket at retirement — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the IRA calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns tax bracket during contribution, derived from the current age, the retirement age and the tax bracket at retirement. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the IRA calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the current age, the retirement age, the tax bracket at retirement and the annual contribution, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter tax bracket during contribution in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Tax bracket during contribution opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the IRA calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
